source.title: Every Ablation Is a Dose: Counterweights and the Semblance of Self-Repair
source.authors: Areeb Ahmad; Pratinav Seth; Vinay Kumar Sankarapu

page_placements.theme: Graded, dose-dependent counter-response: downstream responses scale with the upstream write, so removing the write looks like compensation

record.tranche_reason: The study measures downstream responses to controlled interventions and argues that apparent self-repair is release of pre-existing coupling, refining the interpretation of compensation. Its nested contrastive swaps differ from conventional component ablations.
record.gate_note: The study intervenes on fine-grained weight-space directions and, in the GPT-2 Small IOI experiment, individual heads; it measures direction contributions in the intervened model. It does not ablate whole layers or measure the full output distribution. Rows below cover the reported counterweight examples, the IOI head results, and the LayerNorm audit. Cited prior-study findings are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study perturbs verdict 'cores' with a dose-swept contrastive swap and measures how downstream directions respond. Its λ=−1 rung equals an opposite-class resample. Its results bear on named compensators (counterweight neurons, IOI backup and copy-suppression heads), late-MLP opposition, the LayerNorm account, and how ablations place components. It argues self-repair is release of a standing coupling, so several versions need restating.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that apparent self-repair is passive release of a standing coupling, not a reactive process. Conventional zero, mean or resample ablations are uncalibrated, data-set points on a dose axis. Within |λ|≤1 responses are approximately affine, with slopes anticipated from the weights. Renormalization is excluded for their swap, but they say the LayerNorm mediator remains real for deletion-type ablations. They limit the claims to one verdict task plus IOI.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a nested, prompt-matched contrastive swap of a core direction across a dose ladder and measures downstream total effects with regime-matched interchange patches, rather than conventional zero, mean, or resample ablation. The study argues that ablations correspond to uncontrolled points on its dose axis.
record.method_sensitivity: Responses differ by model, direction, and dose; joint-core interventions can recruit more than single-core interventions. The response saturates beyond full inversion. In GPT-2 Small, L11.h10's curvature depends on whether L10.h7 is clamped with the core.

fits_no_version.finding: A weights-only wiring alignment z_r predicts the rank of the coupling |γ_r| (Spearman 0.55–0.82 per model). On IOI the query channel carries the association (ρ=0.82).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: How strongly a component compensates can be anticipated from static weight alignment with the upstream component's write.

fits_no_version.finding: 16 of 68 certified directions are relays (γ>0) that lose contribution as the core is withdrawn. 52 are counterweights.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream components split into counterweights and relays, with fixed signed gains along a dose axis.

fits_no_version.finding: Affine dose law within |λ|≤1 (out-of-sample R² 0.65–0.91), with saturation beyond full inversion.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compensation is proportional to the displacement of the upstream signal, not a threshold-triggered response.

record.code_released: not stated (the paper says code and per-run outputs will be released with the camera-ready version)
record.problems: Evidence is limited to a zero-shot binary factual-verdict task with model-specific clean-correct pairs and one answer position, plus a small IOI head bench in one model. The main intervention is a controlled contrastive swap rather than a conventional ablation. The study does not test general-text full-distribution recovery, and the fitted affine law is limited to the on-manifold window; the authors report saturation beyond it.

untested.parts: No whole attention-layer ablation or layer-level compensation measure.
Layer-level late-MLP erasure is not tested; only selected single neurons on a binary verdict margin. Removal is by contrastive swap, not ablation.
Heads are studied only on narrow IOI in GPT-2 Small; no general-text, full-distribution head ablation.
Overcorrection beyond the original effect is not measured. Per-prompt spread of compensation is not reported directly.
No self-repair measurement under actual mean or resample ablation; only the swap, plus placement of those clamps on the dose axis.
No comparison of ablation-based importance scores with a direct-effect or other ground-truth measure; the point is argued only.

missing.what: Fraction of erased verdict restored by backups, instruct vs base (instruct 6–13%, base 11–27%)
Gemma L38.n7088 restores 17%/25% of the erased margin at ×1, and flips positive at ×1
Per-pair dose placed by zero/mean clamps: up to |λ|=5.1; 40% vs 8% of IOI pairs off-manifold under mean ablation
The same counterweights are recruited in base checkpoints and under a learned perturbation
Joint-core removal recruits more than either core alone, super-additively at low dose

record.verdict_notes: Linked V2 and V6, which the reader marked untested. V4 links were moved off R1–R8 because direction contributions are not restoration measures, so V4 verdicts rest on text and are listed under missing. Neither original source is this study. Preprint; code not yet released.

versions.untested_parts: No whole attention-layer ablation or layer-level measurement of later attention-layer compensation.
The study does not measure late MLP downregulation of the maximum-likelihood token or whether that erasure shrinks under earlier-component ablation.
The GPT-2 Small experiment measures head effects on a narrow IOI name-choice margin, not compensation on the full output distribution or on general text across model families and sizes.

The study reports prompt-level standard errors but does not characterize how widely compensation varies across individual prompts or test overcorrection relative to the original component effect. Its dose sweeps include overshoot, but that is not a test of V4's overcorrection criterion.
It tests selected MLP directions and IOI heads, plus an audit of final-normalization gain; it does not test all listed mechanisms across models or tasks.

The primary intervention is a prompt-matched contrastive swap, not an empirical test of mean or resample ablation. The paper places conventional clamps on a dose axis but does not report self-repair outcomes under those ablations.
The study argues that ablation can misstate component importance, but does not compare ablation-based importance scores with a direct-effect measure.
